subject: arts-music
essential_question: How can understanding theater, storytelling, and movement help us explain, decide, create, or solve something that matters?
learning_objectives: Apply improvisation boundaries independently in a new representation, text, situation, or design constraint.
Use subject-appropriate evidence or representation to communicate understanding of improvisation boundaries.
Check, revise, or improve work about improvisation boundaries using stated success criteria.
lesson_success_criteria: The learner completes the central task about improvisation boundaries.
The learner gives evidence, reasoning, a model, or a documented process rather than an unsupported answer.
The learner checks or revises the work and can identify a next step.
materials: unit-specific source, model, manipulatives, safe materials, or approved digital tool

Household-accessible route: pencil or pen and scrap paper are enough. For sound or performance work, tap, clap, use spoken syllables, move a finger, or notate silently. Specialized art materials, instruments, paid software, cameras, microphones, and recording devices are optional and never affect credit.
task_brief: This is day 4 of "Theater, Storytelling, and Movement". That is unit 4 in grade 5. Today is an independent application about improvisation boundaries. It takes about 40–60 minutes. It is one day's work, not the whole unit project. Your unit is working toward this: Develop an original short scene, readers theater, or movement story with accessible performance options. Today helps by working on improvisation boundaries. Your unit also covers character and objective, voice and gesture, scene structure, and improvisation boundaries. Today adds real evidence toward your unit project.
primary_task: Make one short original piece using improvisation boundaries. First write what you want it to do. Just one sentence. Write it before you start. Then make it. Now step back and look. Did it work? Point to the one part that makes it work. Point to one part that gets in the way. Fix that second part. Keep both versions. The work must be yours. A grown-up may show you how but must not make it for you. Keep today's work tied to your unit. Today is about improvisation boundaries. It is part of "Theater, Storytelling, and Movement". Later days in this unit cover other things, like character and objective. Before you stop, do this check: In one concise response, show or explain the most important idea about improvisation boundaries; then identify one check that would catch an error or weak claim. In grade 5, finish on your own. Write a reason for each main choice. If there were two ways to do it, say which one you picked and why.

presentation_and_privacy.presentation_options: You choose the audience. Keeping the work entirely to yourself, showing it to one parent or trusted adult, or submitting it as a file with no one watching are all full-credit options. No public performance, exhibition, class presentation, live audience, photograph, camera, or voice recording is required at any point in this task, and choosing the most private option never lowers the score.
presentation_and_privacy.text_or_no_audio_alternative: A written alternative is always available and scores the same. Instead of performing, speaking, or recording, you may submit a written description of what you made or would make, a notated or diagrammed version, a labelled plan, or a written analysis covering the same criteria. Nothing in this task requires a working microphone, camera, or the ability to perform aloud.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any material you did not create yourself must be in the public domain, openly licensed, or used as a short cited excerpt for study — reproduce no more than the point requires, credit the maker and the source, and never copy full lyrics, a complete score, or a whole image and present it as your own.
accessibility_options: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show a worked example or model.
Allow typed, handwritten, spoken, drawn, manipulatives-based, or demonstrated responses when the standard permits.
Offer reduced-copying, extended-time, hidden-timer, movement-break, and low-distraction options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media.
Preserve the learning target while adjusting quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode.
task_accessibility_provisions: This work takes more than one sitting. Ask for a simple checklist with dates so you know what to do next. Keeping track is not part of your grade.
You can take a break, stretch, or come back to this later. That does not lower your score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Allow a pause, break, or alternate response mode without treating it as failure.
Protect hearing, ventilation, tool safety, copyright, cultural context, and respectful representation.
Provide a non-performance or low-audience option when needed without lowering the academic target.

media.suggestion: Optional diagram, map, worked example, source image, demonstration, or short clip supporting improvisation boundaries.
media.fallback: Provide the same information as readable steps, alt text, transcript, tactile/concrete model, or teacher demonstration.

remediation: Reteaching for improvisation boundaries follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for improvisation boundaries, model it with a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the process for improvisation boundaries works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of improvisation boundaries, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking improvisation boundaries mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply improvisation boundaries under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or teach the idea with an original example without completing another learner’s graded work. Treat this as optional depth on improvisation boundaries rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays private by default and uses only original, public-domain, or properly cited material. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
